title: Copy or reference? Telling them apart
intro: Every language has a quiet rule for whether `b = a` or a `for` loop gives you your own copy or a second name for the same thing. Rust has the same three outcomes (a copy, a shared reference, a move), but it writes which one you get into the code. This lesson gives you tests to find the answer in your own language first.

coming_from.go: `for _, p := range people` hands you a copy of each element, so `p.Age++` changes nothing and you write `people[i].Age++` instead. In Rust the loop says which you get: `for p in &people` reads each element, `for p in &mut people` changes it. `range` over an array also copies the whole array first, and over a slice it does not.
coming_from.kotlin: `for (p in people)` gives you the object itself, so `p.age++` changes it, but the loop variable is always a `val`, so `age++` on a number is an error. Rust spells out the object case: `for p in &mut people` changes each item, `for p in &people` reads it.
coming_from.python: Every name in Python leads to an object, so `for p in people: p.age += 1` changes the objects, while `for n in nums: n += 1` changes nothing (an int cannot change; `+=` makes a new one). Rust shows it: `for p in &mut people` changes the items, and `for mut n in nums.iter().copied()` is a copy.
coming_from.typescript: `for (const p of people) p.age++` changes the objects, because `const` fixes the name, not the object, and `for (let n of nums) n++` changes nothing, because numbers are copied. Rust writes the difference in the loop: `&mut people` for the objects themselves, `.iter().copied()` for copies.
coming_from.java: `for (Person p : people)` copies the reference (Java passes references by value), so `p.age++` reaches the object but `p = other` changes only the loop variable. An `int` loop variable is a plain copy. Rust makes the object case visible: `&mut people`.
coming_from.csharp: `foreach` over a `class` list gives you the object, but over a `struct` list it gives you a read-only copy, and `p.Age++` is error CS1654. Rust has no struct/class split: every type holds its value, and `&`/`&mut` in the loop say whether you see the element itself.
coming_from.c: A C loop that copies `people[i]` into a local struct changes only the copy, and `&people[i]` reaches the original. Rust has the same two choices, `.iter().copied()` and `&mut people`, and the compiler checks the pointer.
coming_from.cpp: `for (auto p : v)` copies each element and `for (auto& p : v)` does not: one character apart. In Rust the loop variable of `&mut v` is visibly a `&mut T`, and `p += 1` on it is a compile error until you write `*p`.

notes: In most languages assignment, passing an argument and a loop variable copy the variable's bytes. The question is whether those bytes are the data or an arrow to it. (C++ is the exception: it runs the type's copy constructor.)
In Rust the code shows it. A plain name is a value (copied if the type is `Copy`, moved if not). A `&` or `&mut` is an arrow.
`for x in v` moves the Vec, `for x in &v` borrows each item, and `for x in &mut v` borrows each item so you can change it with `*x`.
`.clone()` is the copy you ask for by name. Types that are `Copy` (numbers, `bool`, `char`, `&T`) copy without it.

gotcha.title: Changing the loop variable
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Java, Python, TypeScript and C++, `age += 1` on a loop variable looks like it adds one to every age. It runs without a complaint, and with objects instead of numbers the same loop would have worked.
gotcha.rust_sees: `for age in &mut ages` gives you `age: &mut i32`, a reference to the element. `age += 1` would add to the reference, which is not defined, so the compiler asks for `*age += 1`.
gotcha.why: Most of the other languages quietly pick one answer: the loop variable is a copy (or a name for an item that cannot change), so the increment is thrown away. That is fine until you meant to change the list, and the program gives no sign. Rust makes you write `*age` for the element, or `.iter().copied()` if you want a copy, so what you wrote says what you meant.

go.says: Go runs this and prints [30 40 50]. `range` gives you a copy of each element, so `age++` changes the copy and the slice is untouched. The compiler does not complain. With `[]Person` the same happens to `p.Age++`; with `[]*Person` it reaches the Person, because the copy is of the pointer. You write `ages[i]++`.

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses: the loop variable of a `for` is a `val`, so `age++` is "'val' cannot be reassigned". You change the list through its index, `ages[i]++`.
kotlin.error:
Main.kt:4:9: error: 'val' cannot be reassigned.
        age++
        ^^^

python.says: Python prints [30, 40, 50]. `age` is a name for each int in turn. `+=` on an int builds a new int and points `age` at it, so the list still holds the old ones.
python.code:
ages = [30, 40, 50]
for age in ages:
    age += 1
print(ages)

typescript.says: TypeScript prints [ 30, 40, 50 ]. `age` holds its own copy of each number. (With `const age` the compiler would refuse `age += 1`.)

java.says: Java prints [30, 40, 50]. An `int` loop variable is a copy of the element, and Java allows you to change it. With objects the variable is a copy of the reference, so changing a field would reach the object.

csharp.says: C# refuses with CS1656: a `foreach` variable is read-only. You change the array through its index, `ages[i]++`.
csharp.error: Program.cs(6,5): error CS1656: Cannot assign to 'age' because it is a 'foreach iteration variable'

c.says: C prints [30, 40, 50], and nobody is surprised: C has no for-each loop, so you wrote the copy `int age = ages[i]` yourself. `ages[i]++` or a pointer `&ages[i]` would change the array. In Rust the loop variable is the part that differs: it is a reference, not a copy you made.

cpp.says: C++ prints [30, 40, 50]. `auto age` is a copy of each element, and g++ with `-Wall -Wextra` says nothing. `auto& age` would be the element itself.

places.py.code:
import copy


class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{self.name} {self.age}"


ages = [30, 40]
for age in ages:
    age += 1  # rebinds the name `age`; the list is not touched
print("ages after for age in ages: age += 1:", ages)

for i in range(len(ages)):
    ages[i] += 1  # assigns into the list
print("ages after ages[i] += 1:", ages)

people = [Person("Ada", 36), Person("Linus", 54)]
for p in people:
    p.age += 1  # p names the object that is in the list
print("people after p.age += 1:", people)


def add_item(items):
    items.append("x")  # changes the caller's list


def replace_items(items):
    items = ["y"]  # rebinds the parameter only


mine = []
add_item(mine)
replace_items(mine)
print("after add_item and replace_items:", mine)

# A slice of a list is a new list
nums = [1, 2, 3]
part = nums[0:2]
part[0] = 99
print("nums after part = nums[0:2]; part[0] = 99:", nums)

# Copies are shallow unless you ask
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = copy.copy(grid)
deep = copy.deepcopy(grid)
grid[0][0] = 99
print("shallow[0][0]:", shallow[0][0], " deep[0][0]:", deep[0][0])
rows = [[0]] * 2  # two names for one inner list
rows[0][0] = 7
print("rows after [[0]] * 2 and rows[0][0] = 7:", rows)

# Closures capture the name, not the value
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print("lambdas in a loop:", [f() for f in fs])

}

types.go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

type Point struct{ X int }

func report(kind string, changedOriginal bool) {
	if changedOriginal {
		fmt.Printf("%-8s shares: the other name sees the change\n", kind)
	} else {
		fmt.Printf("%-8s copy:   the other name is untouched\n", kind)
	}
}

func main() {
	n := 1
	m := n
	m = 99
	report("int", n == 99)

	s := "go"
	t := s
	t = "changed"
	report("string", s == "changed")

	arr := [2]int{1, 2}
	arr2 := arr
	arr2[0] = 99
	report("array", arr[0] == 99)

	pt := Point{1}
	pt2 := pt
	pt2.X = 99
	report("struct", pt.X == 99)

	sl := []int{1, 2}
	sl2 := sl
	sl2[0] = 99
	report("slice", sl[0] == 99)

	mp := map[string]int{"a": 1}
	mp2 := mp
	mp2["a"] = 99
	report("map", mp["a"] == 99)

	p := &Point{1}
	p2 := p
	p2.X = 99
	report("pointer", p.X == 99)

	ch := make(chan int, 1)
	ch2 := ch
	ch2 <- 7
	report("chan", len(ch) == 1)

	count := 0
	f := func() { count++ }
	f2 := f
	f2()
	report("func", count == 1)

	_ = m
	_ = t
}

types.kt.code:
data class Point(var x: Int)

data class Team(val name: String, val members: MutableList<String>)

fun report(kind: String, changed: Boolean) {
    println("%-8s %s".format(kind, if (changed) "shares: the other name sees the change" else "copy:   the other name is untouched"))
}

fun main() {
    var n = 1
    val m = n
    n = 99
    report("Int", m == 99)

    val p = Point(1)
    val q = p
    q.x = 99
    report("object", p.x == 99)

    val list = mutableListOf(1, 2)
    val list2 = list
    list2[0] = 99
    report("List", list[0] == 99)

    // copy() makes a new Point
    val c = p.copy()
    c.x = 5
    println("p.x after changing the copy(): ${p.x}")

    // Identity and equality are different operators
    val r = Point(99)
    println("p === q: ${p === q}  (same object)")
    println("p === r: ${p === r}, p == r: ${p == r}  (same x, different object)")

    // copy() is shallow: the new Team holds the same member list
    val a = Team("red", mutableListOf("ana"))
    val b = a.copy()
    b.members[0] = "zed"
    println("a.members: ${a.members}")

    // A lambda captures the variable itself, so it can change it
    var count = 0
    val inc = { count++ }
    inc()
    inc()

    // A loop variable is a val: you can change the object it names, not the name
    val people = listOf(Point(1), Point(2))
    for (pt in people) {
        pt.x++
    }
    println("people after for (pt in people) pt.x++: $people")

def report(kind, changed):

# Every name leads to an object. "Copy or shared?" is "can that object change?"
n = 1
m = n
m += 1  # an int cannot change: += makes a new int and rebinds m
report("int", n == 2)

s = "hi"
t = s
t += "!"  # a str cannot change either
report("str", s == "hi!")

tup2 = tup
tup2 += (3,)  # a tuple cannot change
report("tuple", tup == (1, 2, 3))

lst2 = lst
lst2 += [3]  # a list can change, and += changes it in place
report("list", lst == [1, 2, 3])

lst3 = lst
lst3 = lst3 + [4]  # + builds a new list and rebinds lst3
print("after lst3 = lst3 + [4], lst is", lst)

d2 = d

report("dict", d["a"] == 99)

q = p
